claims.text: Selective oxidation in AlCrCoFeNi is driven largely by outward Al diffusion.
High oxygen availability in air accelerates Al oxidation.
Heating AlCrCoFeNi in air produces a continuous, adherent duplex scale consisting of external Al2O3 and an inner Cr2O3-rich region.
The duplex oxide formed in air remains coherent above 900 °C under the stated heating conditions.
Low-p(O2) vacuum exposure produces slower oxidation than atmospheric-air exposure.
Vacuum exposure produces only a thin alumina film.
Formation of the duplex oxide suppresses extensive BCC/B2-to-FCC and transient sigma-phase transformation in the substrate.
The as-cast AlCrCoFeNi alloy consists primarily of approximately 79% BCC and 21% ordered B2 phases.
The as-cast alloy has a spinodally decomposed microstructure.
The alloy has an EDS-measured Al concentration of approximately 17.26 at.%.
During heating, the initial BCC/B2 substrate passes through intermediate FCC and Cr-Fe-rich sigma-phase states before sigma dissolves.
Oxidation concurrently generates an Al-rich external Al2O3 scale and a Cr-rich or Cr2O3 inner region.
A properly balanced rate of Al oxidation and scale formation allows the duplex scale to maintain interface stability.
Cr contributes to outward diffusion and oxidation, but less strongly than Al.
Rapid duplex-scale formation in air minimizes further Al depletion in the substrate.
Limiting Al depletion limits destabilizing substrate phase transformations.
The thin alumina film formed under vacuum is less protective than the duplex scale formed in air.
Air exposure is predicted to produce earlier and more extensive oxidation than vacuum exposure.
Air exposure is predicted to produce a thicker multilayer Al2O3/Cr2O3 scale, an Al-depleted subsurface zone, and transient substrate phase modifications.
Significant oxidation begins at approximately 900–1000 °C under the specified non-equilibrium heating conditions.
